concepts.title: Environment as a Political Question
concepts.definition: Environmental concerns entered world politics as the effects of industrial growth - ozone depletion, global warming, resource depletion - crossed borders; since northern states industrialised first, questions of responsibility and equity divide rich and developing countries.
concepts.key_idea: The core clash is distributive: who bears the cost of saving a commons damaged mostly by the industrialised North?
concepts.textbook_ref: leps106.txt environmental concerns and North-South divides sections
question_patterns: name the global environmental issues of the chapter
why do North-South divides shape climate politics
explain the commons argument with examples
state the concerns of developing countries in climate talks
relate industrialisation to ecological footprints
define sustainable development in this context

solution_steps.explain: ozone, warming, biodiversity and resource loss head the agenda
the North industrialised first; the South seeks development space
common but differentiated responsibility frames the fairness debate

concepts.title: Global Commons and Conferences
concepts.definition: The global commons - earth's atmosphere, Antarctica, ocean floor and outer space - lie outside national jurisdiction; the Antarctic Treaty of 1959 reserved the continent for peaceful science, and conferences from Stockholm 1972 to Rio 1992 and Kyoto 1997 built the regime of environmental agreements.
concepts.key_idea: The Kyoto protocol followed the Rio earth summit by the difference of 1997 and 1992.
concepts.textbook_ref: leps106.txt Antarctic Treaty 1959, Stockholm 1972, Rio 1992 and Kyoto 1997 sections
question_patterns: define the global commons and list its components
what does the Antarctic Treaty provide
compute the years between the Rio summit and the Kyoto protocol
state the Stockholm conference's significance
explain common but differentiated responsibilities
evaluate the effectiveness of summit diplomacy

solution_steps.explain: 1997 - 1992 = five years between summit and protocol

concepts.title: Indigenous Peoples and Resource Rights
concepts.definition: Indigenous peoples - whose homelands cross borders and whose cultures predate modern states - seek recognition of land and resource rights; their movements highlight how states and corporations appropriate forests, minerals and knowledge, and the UN declared an international day and decade for them.
concepts.key_idea: Indigenous claims turn environment into justice: protecting cultures means protecting the ecosystems they manage.
concepts.textbook_ref: leps106.txt indigenous peoples' definition, voices and rights sections
question_patterns: who are indigenous peoples and where do they live
what rights do indigenous movements demand
how do states and corporations threaten indigenous lands
state the UN's recognitions of indigenous peoples
relate indigenous knowledge to conservation
give examples of indigenous struggles from the chapter

solution_steps.explain: descendants of original inhabitants across the Americas, Australia and beyond
land titles, cultural survival and resource consent head their agenda
their livelihoods often sustain the very biodiversity states seek to protect

concepts.title: Resource Geopolitics: Oil and Water
concepts.definition: Resources shape world politics: oil concentrates power in West Asia and the control of supply lines, and water - river basins like the Jordan, Tigris-Euphrates and the Indus - generates disputes where upstream and downstream states meet; competition for natural resources remains a driver of conflict.
concepts.key_idea: Whoever commands pipelines, straits and river heads commands leverage: resource geography is power geography.
concepts.textbook_ref: leps106.txt oil politics, water disputes and regional competition sections
question_patterns: explain oil's role in world politics and West Asia
name the river basins prone to water disputes
describe the Indus waters arrangement's significance
relate pipeline routes to geopolitical competition
state the concept of water as a strategic resource
evaluate cooperation possibilities over shared resources

solution_steps.explain: Western Asian reserves and sea lanes anchor energy geopolitics
Jordan and Tigris-Euphrates basins fuel interstate water conflicts
the Indus treaty shows water sharing can survive rivalries

worked_examples.question_pattern: The Rio earth summit was held in 1992 and the Kyoto protocol in 1997. Compute the years between them.
Name the four global commons and why they need treaties.

solution_template.explain: atmosphere, Antarctica, ocean floor and outer space
no state owns them, so each may overuse them
treaties like the Antarctic Treaty create shared rules

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain water as a strategic resource with one river-basin example.

solution_template.explain: upstream states control flow that downstream economies need
Jordan basin disputes tie water to regional conflict
water sharing becomes a test of cooperation, not just engineering
